Analysis of Variance Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/anova.qmd 
library(dplyr)
library(apa7)
library(afex)
library(car)

The apa_anova function makes APA-style analysis of variance (ANOVA) source tables. Like apa_parameters, it relies on the easystats packages to do the computing: parameters::model_parameters gets the sums of squares, F tests, and p-values, and the effectsize package computes effect sizes and their confidence intervals. The workflow is the same as for regression tables:

  1. Fit a model with aov, lm, or one of the afex functions (aov_car, aov_ez, or aov_4).
  2. apa_anova converts the fit object into a tibble.
  3. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, the tibble is displayed as an APA-style table automatically. Pass it to apa_flextable to customize the table or save it.

apa_anova accepts:

Object Example
Between-subjects models aov(y ~ a * b, data), lm(y ~ a * b, data)
Repeated-measures models with error strata aov(y ~ a * b + Error(id / b), data)
afex models afex::aov_ez("id", "y", data, between = "a", within = "b")
ANOVA tables anova(fit), car::Anova(fit, type = 2)

Between-Subjects Designs

A one-way design

In the ToothGrowth data set, guinea pigs were given one of three doses of vitamin C. Does tooth length differ by dose?

d_tooth <- ToothGrowth |>
  mutate(dose = factor(dose)) |> 
  rename(Dose = dose,
         Supplement = supp,
         Length = len)

fit_dose <- aov(Length ~ Dose, data = d_tooth)
apa_anova(fit_dose)

The table has a row for each effect and a row for the error term (the residuals). Its columns are the sums of squares (SS), degrees of freedom (df), mean squares (MS), the F test with its p-value, and eta squared (η2). The default effect size is partial η2, but in a one-way design, partial and non-partial η2 are the same, so the column is labeled η2.

In the console, apa_anova prints as an ordinary tibble, so you can inspect it or post-process it with dplyr. Here as_tibble is used to show that tibble in this document.

apa_anova(fit_dose) |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  Source `*SS*`   `*df*` `*MS*`   `*F*`   `*p*`   `*&eta;*^2^`
  <chr>  <chr>    <chr>  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>   <chr>
1 Dose   2,426.43  2     1,213.22 "67.42" "<.001" ".70"
2 Error  1,025.78 57        18.00 ""      ""      ""

A factorial design

The guinea pigs also received vitamin C either as orange juice or as ascorbic acid (supp). The factorial model tests both main effects and their interaction. Interaction terms are labeled with a multiplication sign (e.g., Supp × Dose).

fit_tooth <- aov(Length ~ Supplement * Dose, data = d_tooth)
apa_anova(fit_tooth)

Choosing columns

The anova_parameters argument selects the columns and their order. "Effect_Size" stands for whichever effect size is selected (see below), and "CI" adds its confidence interval. Columns are labeled by apa_anova automatically.

apa_anova(

  anova_parameters = c("Parameter", "df", "F", "p", "Effect_Size")

Effect Sizes

Choosing an effect size

By default, apa_anova displays partial eta squared (η2p), the most commonly reported effect size in psychology. Partial η2 is the proportion of variance explained by an effect after the variance explained by the other effects is set aside. Other effect sizes are available with the effect_size, partial, and generalized arguments:

Arguments Effect size
effect_size = "eta" (default) partial η2 (η2p)
effect_size = "eta", partial = FALSE η2
effect_size = "eta", generalized = TRUE generalized η2 (η2G)
effect_size = "omega" ω2p
effect_size = "omega", partial = FALSE partial ω2 (ω2p)
effect_size = "epsilon" partial ε2 (ε2p)
effect_size = NULL no effect size

η2 overestimates the population effect size in small samples. ω2 and ε2 are less biased, so they are good choices for small samples.

apa_anova(fit_tooth, effect_size = "omega")

Generalized η2 (Olejnik & Algina, 2003) is comparable across designs with different numbers of between- and within-subjects factors, which makes it useful for meta-analysis and for comparing studies. It is the default effect size in afex.

Confidence intervals

APA style recommends reporting confidence intervals for effect sizes. Add "CI" to anova_parameters to show them.

apa_anova(
  fit_tooth,
  anova_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", "df", "F", "p", "Effect_Size", "CI"
  ),
  ci = 0.90
)

Intervals are two-sided. Because F tests are one-sided, a 90% interval is a natural companion to an F test with α = .05: the interval excludes 0 if and only if the F test is significant (Steiger, 2004). Its lower bound is 0 when the test is not significant. Set ci = 0.95 for 95% intervals.

Intervals are not shown for generalized η2, because the intervals computed by effectsize for it can exclude the point estimate. If you request them, apa_anova gives a warning and leaves them out.

Unbalanced Designs and Types of Sums of Squares

When cell sizes are unequal, the effects in a factorial design are correlated, and the sums of squares depend on how the variance they share is divided. In the Moore data set from the carData package, participants were paired with a partner of high or low status, and the number of times they conformed to their partner’s judgments was recorded. Participants’ authoritarianism was classified as low, medium, or high. The cell sizes are unequal:

d_moore <- carData::Moore |>
  mutate(
    fcategory = factor(fcategory, levels = c("low", "medium", "high")),
    partner.status = factor(partner.status, levels = c("low", "high"))
  ) |>
  rename(
    Authoritarianism = fcategory,
    `Authoritarianism Score` = fscore,
    `Partner Status` = partner.status
  )

table(d_moore$Authoritarianism, d_moore$`Partner Status`)

         low high
  low     10    5
  medium   4   11
  high     8    7

By default, apa_anova uses Type 1 (sequential) sums of squares, as anova and summary.aov do. Each effect is adjusted only for the effects entered before it, so the results depend on the order of the terms in the formula.

fit_moore <- lm(conformity ~ Authoritarianism * `Partner Status`, data = d_moore)
apa_anova(fit_moore)

Type 3 tests adjust each effect for all other effects, including interactions. Type 3 tests are meaningful only when factors are coded with contrasts that sum to zero (e.g., contr.sum), not with R’s default treatment contrasts, so set the contrasts before fitting the model:

fit_moore_sum <- lm(
  conformity ~ Authoritarianism * `Partner Status`,
  data = d_moore,
  contrasts = list(Authoritarianism = contr.sum, `Partner Status` = contr.sum)
)
apa_anova(fit_moore_sum, type = 3)

Analysis of Covariance

An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) is an ANOVA with one or more continuous covariates. Fit it with lm or aov. Here, partner status is tested while controlling for participants’ authoritarianism scores. Type 2 sums of squares adjust each effect for the other, regardless of the order of the terms.

fit_ancova <- lm(conformity ~ `Authoritarianism Score` + `Partner Status`, data = d_moore)
apa_anova(fit_ancova, type = 2)

Repeated-Measures Designs

Error strata with aov

In the obk.long data set from the afex package (O’Brien & Kaiser, 1985), 16 participants in three treatment groups were measured before treatment, after treatment, and at follow-up. Each phase had five measurements, which we average here.

d_obk <- obk.long |>
  mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("pre", "post", "fup"))) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .by = c(id, treatment, phase)) |>
  rename(Treatment = treatment, Phase = phase)

In base R, a mixed design with a between-subjects factor (treatment) and a within-subjects factor (phase) is fit with aov and an Error term. Each error stratum has its own error term. apa_anova introduces each stratum with a heading row and indents its effects.

fit_obk_aov <- aov(value ~ Treatment * Phase + Error(id / Phase), data = d_obk)
apa_anova(fit_obk_aov)

With aov, sums of squares are Type 1, and no correction is made for violations of sphericity.

afex models

The afex package fits repeated-measures ANOVAs with Type 3 sums of squares and corrects the degrees of freedom of within-subjects effects for violations of sphericity (Greenhouse–Geisser by default). In afex models, each effect has its own error term, so the table shows the degrees of freedom of each effect and its error term (dfeffect and dferror) and the mean squared error (MSE), as afex’s nice function does. As in afex, generalized η2 is the default effect size.

fit_obk <- aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "value",
  data = d_obk,
  between = "Treatment",
  within = "Phase"
)
apa_anova(fit_obk)

  generalized = FALSE,
  anova_parameters = c(

The sphericity correction is set when the model is fit or printed in afex (e.g., afex_options(correction_aov = "none")).

Customizing ANOVA Tables

Notes

The table does not say which type of sums of squares or which sphericity correction was used, so say so in a table note. apa_anova records how the table was made, and apa_note turns that record into note text:

tbl_moore <- apa_anova(fit_moore, type = 2)
apa_note(tbl_moore)
[1] "Type II sums of squares. *&eta;*^2^~p~ = partial eta squared."

The note says which type of sums of squares was used and defines the effect size. For afex models, it also says which effects have sphericity-corrected degrees of freedom. afex corrects only effects that involve a within-subjects factor with more than two levels, so the note names those factors:

tbl_obk <- apa_anova(fit_obk, starred = "F")
apa_note(tbl_obk)
[1] "Type III sums of squares. Degrees of freedom and *p*-values for effects involving Phase are Greenhouse–Geisser corrected. *MSE* = mean square error; *&eta;*^2^~G~ = generalized eta squared. ^\\* ^*p* < .05. ^\\*\\* ^*p* < .01. ^\\*\\*\\* ^*p* < .001."

When stars or bold values are used, the note explains them, after the general notes as APA style requires. The text is in markdown, and it does not start with “Note.” because apaquarto adds that.

With apaquarto, use apa_note in the apa-note chunk option with !expr. Chunk options are evaluated before the chunk runs, so make the table in an earlier chunk (as tbl_obk was made above) and display it in the chunk with the note. Write it as apa7::apa_note, because in documents with cached chunks, chunk options can be evaluated before library(apa7) takes effect:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-obk
#| tbl-cap: Mixed ANOVA of Treatment and Phase
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_obk)
tbl_obk
```
Note. Type III sums of squares. Degrees of freedom and p-values for effects involving Phase are Greenhouse–Geisser corrected. MSE = mean square error; η2G = generalized eta squared. * p < .05. ** p < .01. *** p < .001.

Without apaquarto, apa_flextable(tbl, note = TRUE) puts the same note below the table (or pass your own text as note). Do not combine it with the apa-note chunk option, or the note will appear twice.

The generated note is a starting point. To add to it, combine it with your own text (e.g., paste(apa_note(tbl_obk), "Outliers were removed.")). With collapse = NULL, apa_note returns one sentence per element, so you can drop or reword sentences.

apa_note reads an attribute of the table. dplyr functions such as mutate and filter keep it, but some operations (e.g., joins) drop it, so call apa_note on the table that apa_anova returned.

Labels and post-processing

Variable names are converted to title case (e.g., supp becomes Supp). For better labels, rename the variables before fitting the model, as was done for the Moore data above. Because the output is a tibble, you can also change the labels afterward.

Further formatting is available with apa_flextable.

apa_anova(fit_tooth) |>
  apa_flextable(table_width = .8)

Model comparisons

apa_anova makes source tables. To compare nested models (e.g., anova(m1, m2)), use apa_performance_comparison or pass a list of models to apa_parameters, as described in the regression article.

Using apa_parameters

apa_parameters returns the same table for aov and afex models, so apa_parameters(fit) and apa_anova(fit) are interchangeable for these models. To display the regression coefficients of an ANOVA model, fit it with lm and use apa_parameters.

References

O’Brien, R. G., & Kaiser, M. K. (1985). MANOVA method for analyzing repeated measures designs: An extensive primer. Psychological Bulletin, 97(2), 316–333. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.97.2.316

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2003). Generalized eta and omega squared statistics: Measures of effect size for some common research designs. Psychological Methods, 8(4), 434–447. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.8.4.434

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164
